problems.title: Net Climb Stretches
problems.story: A cycling club logs the climb of every road segment on its Sunday loop, in metres, with descents written as negative numbers. For a training plan the coach wants to know how many stretches of the loop gain exactly a chosen amount of height, so riders can repeat a stretch of the right difficulty.
problems.statement:
You are given a target net climb, followed by the climb of each road segment in riding order. A climb can be positive, negative (a descent) or zero.

A stretch is a run of one or more neighbouring segments, and its net climb is the sum of their climbs.

Return how many stretches have a net climb exactly equal to the target.
problems.inputFormat: The first number is the target net climb. Every number after it is the climb of one segment, in riding order. There is at least one segment.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the number of stretches whose climbs add up to exactly the target.

parameters.name: changes
parameters.description: The climb of each segment in metres, negative for a descent.

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: The net climb a stretch must add up to.

constraints: The answer can be larger than 2^31 - 1

examples.explanation: Three stretches add up to 3: segments 0 and 1 (1 + 2), segment 3 alone, and segments 3 and 4 (3 + 0). The flat last segment makes the last two different stretches with the same climb.
Each of the three pairs of neighbours cancels out, and all four segments together cancel out too: four stretches.
The whole loop climbs only 3, so no stretch can reach 5.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
Neighbouring pairs cancel, and so does the whole ride.
One segment that is exactly the target.
One segment that misses the target.
Five thousand segments at the largest climb; only the whole ride reaches the target.
Extreme climbs and descents alternating, with a negative target.
Four thousand flat segments: every one of the 8,002,000 stretches has net climb 0.
The same running total recurs many times, so each occurrence must be counted, not just remembered.
Zero-sum stretches that start and end in the middle of the ride, which a two-pointer window cannot find with negative climbs.
Five thousand random climbs; quadratic work is twelve million additions.

hints: Checking every pair of start and end segments is correct but quadratic. What does the climb of a stretch look like in terms of running totals?
If P(j) is the total climb of the first j segments, the stretch from segment i to segment j - 1 climbs P(j) - P(i).

Walk the ride once, keeping a count of how often each running total has appeared. At each step, the number of stretches ending here is the count of earlier running totals equal to the current total minus the target.

editorial.overview: A stretch's net climb is a difference of two running totals. Counting stretches with climb k therefore means counting pairs of running totals that differ by k, which a hash map does in one pass. Two pointers do not work here, because descents make the window sum go up and down.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Fix each start segment and extend the end one segment at a time, adding the climb and counting every time the sum equals the target. That is O(n^2): five billion additions at the largest size.
editorial.optimalApproach: Keep a running total P and a map from each running total seen so far to how many times it has been seen, starting with {0: 1} for the empty prefix. For each segment, add its climb to P, add map[P - target] to the answer, then increment map[P]. Running totals stay within 10^9 in absolute value, and the answer within n(n + 1) / 2, so 64-bit integers suffice.
editorial.correctnessProof: Let P(0) = 0 and P(j) be the total climb of the first j segments. The stretch of segments i to j - 1 has climb P(j) - P(i), so it has climb k exactly when P(i) = P(j) - k. Every stretch corresponds to exactly one pair i < j. When the algorithm processes segment j - 1, the map holds the counts of P(0) to P(j - 1), so it adds exactly the number of i < j with P(i) = P(j) - k. Summing over j counts every qualifying pair once.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n) expected, with one hash-map lookup and update per segment.
editorial.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the map of running totals.

problems.title: Solar Output Streak
problems.story: A school logs the output of its rooftop solar panel every day. The science teacher wants a short project window: the fewest consecutive days in the log that together produced enough energy to run the lab for a term.
problems.statement:
You are given a target amount of energy, followed by the energy the panel produced on each day, in order. Every day's output is positive.

A streak is a run of one or more consecutive days. Return the number of days in the shortest streak whose outputs add up to at least the target. If even all the days together fall short of the target, return 0.
problems.inputFormat: The first number is the target amount of energy. Every number after it is one day's output, in date order. There is at least one day.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the length of the shortest streak that reaches the target, or 0 if no streak does.

parameters.name: output
parameters.description: The energy produced on each day, in date order.

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: The energy a streak must reach.

examples.explanation: No two neighbouring days reach 11 (the best pair is 6 + 4 = 10), but three days do, for example 5 + 1 + 6 = 12. The answer is 3.
The three days produce only 12 together, so no streak reaches 20.
The first day alone produces 7, which already meets the target.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
All the days together fall short, so the answer is 0.
One day that exactly meets the smallest target.
The largest target against six thousand maximal days: still short, so 0.
Only all six thousand days together reach the target.
Equal days: the answer is the target divided by the daily output, rounded up.
A long weak run followed by one day that meets the target alone: the window must shrink all the way to one day.
The shortest streak is in the middle, not at either end.
Seven thousand random days and a target that needs about fifty of them.

hints: Because every output is positive, adding a day to a streak always increases its total, and removing one always decreases it.
Grow a window on the right until it reaches the target, then shrink it from the left for as long as it still does.
Every time the window reaches the target, record its length before shrinking. Each day enters and leaves the window at most once.

editorial.overview: With positive outputs, the window total grows when the right end moves and shrinks when the left end moves. That monotonic behaviour lets a two-pointer sliding window examine, for every right end, the shortest qualifying window ending there, in linear time.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: For each start day, add days until the total reaches the target and record the length. That is O(n^2) in the worst case, when the target is large.
editorial.optimalApproach: Keep a left pointer and a running total. For each day r, add its output. While the total is at least the target, record r - left + 1 if it is shorter than the best so far, then subtract output[left] and move left forward. Return the best, or 0 if no window ever reached the target. Totals stay below 10^9 + 10^4, inside 32-bit signed range, but a 64-bit total is used anyway.
editorial.correctnessProof: Fix a right end r and let L(r) be the largest left end such that days L(r) to r reach the target. L(r) never decreases as r grows, because adding day r + 1 only raises totals. The inner loop moves left exactly until the window stops reaching the target, recording each qualifying window on the way, so it records the window from L(r) to r, the shortest one ending at r. Taking the minimum over all r gives the shortest qualifying streak, and if none exists the best stays 0.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n): each pointer moves at most n times.

problems.title: Carousel Tag Count
problems.story: A gift shop keeps its price tags on a spinning display stand, arranged from cheapest to dearest all the way round. At closing time the stand stops wherever it likes, and the clerk reads the tags from the one in front of her. The manager wants to know how many items carry a particular price.
problems.statement:
You are given a target price, followed by the prices on the stand as the clerk read them.

Read from the right starting tag, the prices never decrease, and that starting tag can be anywhere. In other words, the list is a non-decreasing list that has been rotated: some first part of it was moved to the end. Prices can repeat.

Return how many tags carry exactly the target price.
problems.inputFormat: The first number is the target price. Every number after it is the price on one tag, in the order the clerk read them. There is at least one tag.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: how many tags equal the target price.

parameters.name: tags
parameters.description: The prices as read, a rotated non-decreasing list.

constraints: tags is a rotation of a non-decreasing list

examples.explanation: The stand stopped between 9 and 1; read from 1 the prices are 1 3 4 4 5 6 7 9. The price 4 appears twice.
No tag carries the price 8, so the count is 0.
All five tags carry 2. With every price equal, every tag is a valid place to start reading.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
A price that is not on the stand at all.
One tag, and it matches.
One tag, and it does not match.
Prices at both limits, with the largest price repeated just before the seam.
Four thousand tags across the whole range; the smallest possible price appears three times.
The target sits on both sides of the seam, so both sorted parts must be counted.
Almost every tag is equal, which hides the seam from a plain comparison with the middle.
The seam is at the very last tag, and the middle equals the last tag.
A target larger than every price.
Six thousand tags drawn from about a hundred prices, so long runs repeat.
Five thousand distinct-looking prices, rotated by one, target absent.

hints: The list is made of two sorted pieces. If you knew where the second piece starts, you could count the target in each piece with two binary searches.
Compare the middle tag with the last tag of the current range. If the middle is larger, the start of the sorted order is to its right; if smaller, it is at the middle or to its left.

When the middle equals the last tag you cannot tell which side the start is on. Check whether the last tag is itself the start (the tag before it is larger); if not, it is safe to drop the last tag from the range.

editorial.overview: Find the index where the sorted order begins, then count the target in each of the two sorted pieces with lower- and upper-bound binary searches. Repeated prices make the first step need care: when the middle equals the end of the range, the comparison says nothing about where the seam is.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Scan every tag and count matches. That is O(n) and correct; it ignores the order the list is in. The binary-search method is faster whenever repeats are not overwhelming.
editorial.optimalApproach: Search for the start s in [0, n - 1] with lo and hi. While lo < hi, let mid = (lo + hi) / 2. If tags[mid] > tags[hi], set lo = mid + 1. If tags[mid] < tags[hi], set hi = mid. If they are equal and hi > 0 and tags[hi - 1] > tags[hi], hi is the start, so set lo = hi and stop; otherwise set hi = hi - 1. Then s = lo. The pieces tags[s..n-1] and tags[0..s-1] are each sorted, so count the target in each as upper bound minus lower bound, and add.
editorial.correctnessProof: Unless all prices are equal, the cyclic sequence has exactly one descent, and the start s is the index right after it. The search keeps s inside [lo, hi]. If tags[mid] > tags[hi], the descent lies between mid and hi, so s is in (mid, hi]. If tags[mid] < tags[hi], the indices mid to hi are in order with no descent, so s is in [lo, mid]. If they are equal and the descent is just before hi, then s = hi. Otherwise hi is not the start, so s is in [lo, hi - 1]. When lo = hi the range holds only s. If all prices are equal, any start gives a sorted reading. Each piece is sorted, so the two bound searches count exactly the tags equal to the target in it.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(log n) when repeats are limited; O(n) in the worst case, such as many equal prices hiding the seam.

problems.title: Rooftop Rain Pockets
problems.story: An architect is checking a stepped concrete roof for the monsoon. Seen from the side, the roof is a row of one-metre-wide columns of different heights. After a storm, water collects in the dips between taller columns, and the architect needs the total volume that can pond before it all drains off the ends.
problems.statement:
You are given the height of each column of the roof, from left to right. Every column is one unit wide.

After heavy rain, water settles above a column up to the lower of the tallest column to its left and the tallest column to its right, counting the column itself on each side. Water at the two ends runs off the roof.

Return the total amount of water held above all columns.
problems.inputFormat: Every number is the height of one column, from left to right. There is at least one column.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the total units of water the roof holds.

parameters.name: heights
parameters.description: The height of each column, left to right.

constraints: The answer can be larger than 2^31 - 1

examples.explanation: Between the walls of height 2 and 3, the cell of height 0 holds 2 units. Between the wall of 3 and the final wall of 4, water rises to level 3, so the cells of heights 1, 0 and 2 hold 2, 3 and 1 units. That is 8 in all.
The roof only slopes down, so every drop runs off: 0.
Both ends are 4 high, so the two middle cells fill to level 4 and hold 3 units each.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
A roof that only slopes down holds nothing.
A single column holds no water.
Two flat cells at height 0.
Two walls at the largest height with three thousand empty cells between them: 300,000,000 units.
Flat tops of equal height on both sides; the equal walls must not be counted twice.
Repeated equal walls with a pocket between each pair.
A tall wall on the left but a low wall on the right: the water level is set by the lower side.
Pockets inside pockets, which a stack resolves layer by layer.
Six thousand random heights up to the limit.

hints: The water above a column is min(tallest to the left, tallest to the right) minus its own height. Computing both maxima for every column separately is quadratic.
Instead of column by column, think of water filling in horizontal layers between a left wall and a right wall.

Keep a stack of column indices with non-increasing heights. When a taller column arrives, pop the floor of a pocket; the new top of the stack is the left wall and the current column is the right wall.

editorial.overview: Water is held in pockets bounded by a left wall and a right wall. A monotonic stack finds every pocket the moment its right wall appears, and adds the water in horizontal layers. A two-pointer version that walks in from both ends is an equally good alternative.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: For each column, scan left and right for the tallest columns and add min(left, right) - height. That is O(n^2).
editorial.optimalApproach: Scan left to right with a stack of indices whose heights do not increase from bottom to top. For column i, while the stack is non-empty and heights[top] < heights[i]: pop the top as the floor. If the stack is now empty there is no left wall, so stop. Otherwise the left wall is the new top l, the width is i - l - 1, and the layer height is min(heights[l], heights[i]) - heights[floor]; add width times layer height. Then push i. Equal heights are not popped, so a flat stretch forms a single floor and is not counted twice. Totals reach at most 10^10, so use 64-bit integers.
editorial.correctnessProof: Each time a floor is popped, the columns strictly between l and i are no higher than the floor, because they were popped earlier. The water between l and i above height heights[floor] and up to min(heights[l], heights[i]) is held, since walls of at least that height stand at l and i, and none of it was counted before, because earlier layers lay below heights[floor]. Conversely, every unit of held water above column j at level t lies between the nearest columns on each side that reach level t; the column that ends the layer below t is popped exactly when the right one of those arrives, and that pop counts the unit. So every unit is counted exactly once.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n): every index is pushed and popped at most once.

problems.title: Courier Route Merge
problems.story: A delivery company plans its routes as chains of stops: from each stop there is exactly one next stop, until a stop that ends the line. Two couriers set out from different depots. Dispatch wants the first stop where the second courier could hand a parcel to the first, which is the first stop on the first courier's route that the second courier also passes.
problems.statement:
You are given the starting stop of the second courier, followed by, for every stop, the stop a courier goes to next, or -1 if that stop ends the line. Stops are numbered from 0, and the first courier starts at stop 0. Following the next stops from any stop always reaches -1: there are no loops.

Each courier passes through its own starting stop and then follows the next stops. Return the first stop on the first courier's route that the second courier also passes through, or -1 if the two routes share no stop.
problems.inputFormat: The first number is the second courier's starting stop. Every number after it is the next stop of stops 0, 1, 2 and so on, with -1 marking the end of a line.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the first shared stop along the first courier's route, or -1.

parameters.name: nextStop
parameters.description: For each stop, the next stop, or -1 at the end of a line.

constraints: Any number of stops may share the same next stop
A solution using constant extra memory exists

examples.explanation: The first courier rides 0, 2, 4 and the second rides 3, 1, 4. Stop 4 is the first stop of the first route that the second route also visits.
Each route is a single stop, and the two stops are different.
The first courier rides 0, 1, 2. The second courier starts at stop 2, the end of that route, so they share stop 2.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
Two one-stop routes that never meet.
One stop, and both couriers start on it.
A single six-thousand-stop line; the second courier starts at its last stop.
Two routes of three thousand stops that only meet at the very last stop.
Nine stops all lead to stop 9, so the value 9 repeats throughout the list.
Three stops share the next stop 3, and the routes merge there.
The second courier starts just before stop 0, so the first courier's starting stop is the answer.
Routes of very different lengths; matching stops by position without aligning the lengths gives the wrong stop.
Eight thousand stops in a random network with no loops.

hints: Once two routes reach the same stop they never separate again, because every stop has only one next stop. So the shared part is a common tail.
If both routes had the same length, you could walk them side by side until the couriers stand on the same stop.
Measure both route lengths first, advance the courier on the longer route by the difference, then walk both one stop at a time until they meet or both reach -1.

editorial.overview: Each stop has one next stop, so two routes that meet share everything from the meeting stop to the end: they form a Y shape. Aligning the two routes by length and walking them in step finds the meeting stop with constant extra memory, the same idea as finding where two linked lists intersect.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Mark every stop on the second route in a set, then walk the first route and return the first marked stop. That is O(n) time but O(n) extra memory.
editorial.optimalApproach: Walk from stop 0 to the end to get the first route's length la, and from start to get lb. Advance the longer route's pointer by |la - lb| stops. Then advance both pointers together until they are equal; return that stop, which is -1 if they both run off the end without meeting. Both walks visit each stop at most twice.
editorial.correctnessProof: If the routes share any stop, let m be the first stop of the first route that lies on the second. From m onward both routes coincide, because each stop has a unique successor, so the routes have equal-length tails from m to the end and the parts before m are disjoint. After skipping the length difference, both pointers are the same number of stops from the end, so they reach m on the same step and cannot be equal before it, as their earlier stops are disjoint. If the routes share no stop, the pointers are never equal on a stop and both become -1 on the same step, which is returned.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n): at most two walks over each route.

problems.title: Gallery Tour Order
problems.story: A gallery's rooms are laid out like a binary search tree of room numbers: from every room, the left door leads to lower-numbered rooms and the right door to higher-numbered ones. Guides always tour in the same pattern, visiting a room and then everything through its left door before everything through its right door. A visitor handed in a list of rooms she says a guide showed her, and the curator wants to know whether some layout makes it a genuine tour.
problems.statement:
You are given a list of room numbers. Decide whether it is the preorder of some binary search tree: the root first, then the whole left subtree in preorder, then the whole right subtree in preorder.

In this tree, every room in a node's left subtree has a smaller number than the node, and every room in its right subtree has a number greater than or equal to it. Repeated numbers are allowed and always sit to the right.

Return 1 if some such tree has exactly this preorder, otherwise 0.
problems.inputFormat: Every number is one room number, in the order the guide visited them. There is at least one room.
problems.outputFormat: Return 1 if the list is a valid preorder, otherwise 0.

parameters.name: rooms
parameters.description: The room numbers in visiting order.

constraints: Equal room numbers go into the right subtree

examples.explanation: 8 is the root. 5, 1 and 7 form its left subtree (1 left of 5, 7 right of 5), and 10 with 12 to its right forms the right subtree.
Once the tour reaches 9, it is in the right subtree of 8, where every room must be at least 8. Room 7 cannot appear there.
Each repeated 4 goes to the right of the one before, so the tree is a single path to the right.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
A smaller room after the walk has turned right at the root.
One room is always a valid tour.
Room numbers at both limits.
Five thousand rooms in falling order: a tree that is one long left path.
Repeated 5s must all hang to the right of the first 5.
After the walk turns right into an equal room, a smaller room can no longer appear.
Every room is in order with its neighbour, but 7 comes after the walk has passed 10.
The last 2 is allowed: equal rooms go right, so it sits in the right subtree of the root 2 and the left subtree of 3. A check that treats an equal room as too small rejects it wrongly.
The preorder of a random five-thousand-room tree with repeated numbers.
The same tour with two neighbouring rooms swapped late in the walk.

hints: In a preorder, once the walk moves into the right subtree of a room x, every later room must be at least x. That bound only ever rises.
Keep a stack of rooms whose right subtree has not been entered yet. Their numbers decrease from bottom to top.
For each room: if it is below the current lower bound, the answer is 0. Otherwise pop every stacked room that is less than or equal to it, raising the bound to the last one popped, then push it.

editorial.overview: Reading a preorder left to right, the walk goes down left edges until it turns right at some ancestor, after which nothing smaller than that ancestor may appear. A monotonic stack tracks the ancestors still waiting for their right turn, and a single lower bound records the most recent turn.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Rebuild the tree recursively: the first room is the root, the left subtree is the longest following run of smaller rooms, and the rest must all be at least the root; recurse on both parts. That is O(n^2) on a tree that is one long path.
editorial.optimalApproach: Keep low = minus infinity and an empty stack. For each room x: if x < low, return 0. While the stack is non-empty and its top is <= x, set low to the popped top. Push x. If every room passes, return 1. Popping on equality is what sends equal rooms to the right.
editorial.correctnessProof: Invariant: the stack holds, from bottom to top in strictly decreasing order, the rooms on the current root-to-node path whose right subtrees have not started, and low is the largest room whose right subtree contains the current position. A new room x belongs in the right subtree of the deepest stacked room y with y <= x, or in the left subtree of the top if the top is larger than x. Popping exactly the rooms <= x finds that y, and x must be at least every room whose right subtree it is in, which is the new low. If x < low, x would have to be in a right subtree of a room larger than it, which no tree allows, so the list is invalid. If no room ever fails, the stack choices describe a tree with exactly this preorder.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n): each room is pushed and popped at most once.

problems.title: Scrap Press Remnant
problems.story: A recycling yard feeds its scrap blocks through a press two at a time. The press always grabs the two heaviest blocks in the pile, and the yard manager wants to know what will be left at the end of the shift.
problems.statement:
You are given the weight of each scrap block in the pile.

While at least two blocks remain, the press takes the two heaviest blocks. If they weigh the same, both are destroyed. Otherwise the lighter one is destroyed and the heavier one goes back into the pile, now weighing the difference between the two.

Return the weight of the block that is left at the end, or 0 if no block is left.
problems.inputFormat: Every number is the weight of one scrap block. There is at least one block.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the weight of the last block, or 0 if none is left.

parameters.name: weights
parameters.description: The weight of each scrap block.

constraints: When several blocks tie for heaviest, it does not matter which two the press takes

examples.explanation: Press 9 and 6, leaving 3; the pile is 3 5 3. Press 5 and 3, leaving 2; the pile is 3 2. Press 3 and 2, leaving a block of 1.
The two blocks weigh the same, so both are destroyed and nothing is left.
Two of the 4s destroy each other. The third block is never pressed and is left over.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
Two equal blocks destroy each other and nothing is left.
A single block is never pressed, so it is what remains.
Two blocks of different weight leave their difference.
An odd number of blocks at the largest weight: pairs cancel and one block is left.
The four equal heavy blocks cancel in pairs, leaving the light one.
Splitting the blocks into two equal-weight piles would leave nothing, but the press must take the two heaviest every time, and that leaves a block of 2.
The remnant of each press is still the heaviest block, so it has to go back into the pile and be pressed again.
Seven thousand random weights.

hints: There is no choice to make: the rule says exactly which two blocks are pressed. The work is finding the two heaviest quickly, again and again.
Sorting once is not enough, because the remnant of a press can be heavier than other blocks in the pile.
Keep the blocks in a max-heap. Pop two, push back their difference if it is not zero, and stop when at most one block is left.

editorial.overview: This is a direct simulation. The only question is how to find the two heaviest blocks each round, and a max-heap answers that in logarithmic time per operation.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Scan the whole pile for the heaviest block, remove it, and scan again for the next heaviest. Each round costs O(n) and there are up to n rounds, so O(n^2) overall.
editorial.optimalApproach: Push every weight into a max-heap. While the heap holds two or more blocks, pop a and then b, so a >= b. If a > b, push a - b. Finally return the top of the heap, or 0 if it is empty. In languages whose heap is a min-heap, store negated weights or pass a reversed comparator.
editorial.correctnessProof: The heap always holds exactly the blocks in the pile, so its two largest entries are the two blocks the press takes. Each round removes at least one block, so the loop ends, and when it does the heap holds the single remaining block or nothing. Ties do not matter: pressing any two blocks of the heaviest weight produces the same multiset of remaining weights.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n log n): building the heap is O(n), and there are fewer than n rounds of O(log n) work.

problems.title: Workshop Build Order
problems.story: A furniture workshop breaks every order into numbered build steps. Some steps have to wait for others: the frame before the upholstery, the glue before the clamps come off. The foreman suspects some of the written rules contradict each other and wants to know how many steps can actually be finished.
problems.statement:
You are given the number of build steps, followed by a list of ordering rules. Steps are numbered from 0. Each rule is written as two step numbers a and b, meaning step a must be finished before step b can start. A rule can name the same step twice, and the same rule can appear more than once.

A step can be started, and then finished, once every step that its rules say must come before it is finished. Steps with no rules before them can start straight away.

Return how many steps can eventually be finished.
problems.inputFormat: The first number is how many build steps there are. The numbers after it come in pairs, one pair per rule: the step that must come first, then the step that must wait for it. There may be no rules at all.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the number of steps that can be finished.

parameters.name: rules
parameters.description: Ordering rules as consecutive pairs: the earlier step, then the later step.

parameters.name: steps
parameters.description: How many build steps there are.

examples.explanation: Steps 3 and 4 each wait for the other, so neither can ever start. Steps 0, 1, 2 and 5 can be finished in that order.
There are no rules, so all three steps can be finished.
Step 2 must be finished before it starts, which is impossible, and step 3 waits for step 2. Only steps 0 and 1 can be finished.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
No ordering rules at all, so every step can be finished.
One step with no rules.
One step that must come after itself can never start.
The largest number of steps, almost all of them free of rules.
Six thousand steps in one long chain, with the rules listed from the end of the chain back to the start.
The same rule repeated several times still only needs the earlier step once; every step finishes.
Steps 0 and 1 wait for each other, and steps 2 and 3 wait behind them. Counting only the steps on the loop as stuck gives the wrong answer.
Step 2 needs both 0 and 1. Starting it once any one of its earlier steps is done would count it wrongly.
Nine thousand steps and about four and a half thousand random rules, a few of which close loops.

hints: Think of each rule as an arrow from the earlier step to the later one. A step can be finished exactly when no loop of arrows leads into it.
Count, for every step, how many rules it is still waiting on. The steps waiting on nothing can be finished first.
Finishing a step lowers the waiting count of every step it points to. Keep a queue of steps whose count has reached zero; the number of steps that ever enter the queue is the answer.

editorial.overview: The rules form a directed graph. Steps that can be finished are exactly those that Kahn's topological sort removes; any step on a loop, or downstream of one, never reaches zero remaining prerequisites.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Sweep over all steps repeatedly, finishing any step whose earlier steps are all finished, until a full sweep finishes nothing. A long chain listed backwards can need one sweep per step, so this is O(V x (V + E)).
editorial.optimalApproach: Build an adjacency list from each earlier step to its later steps, keeping repeated rules, and count each step's incoming rules. Put every step with a count of zero in a queue. Pop a step, count it, and for each rule leaving it decrease the target's count, queuing the target when its count reaches zero. Return how many steps were popped. A self-rule adds to a step's own count, and only finishing that same step could remove it, so the step never enters the queue.
editorial.correctnessProof: A step enters the queue only when every rule pointing into it has been discharged by finishing its source, so every popped step can really be finished. Conversely, suppose some step s can be finished but is never popped. Among the steps that must be finished before s (including s), take one, t, that is never popped but all of whose earlier steps are popped. Every rule into t comes from a popped step and was discharged, so t's count reached zero and t was queued, a contradiction. So the popped steps are exactly the finishable ones.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(V + E): every step is queued at most once and every rule is processed once.
editorial.spaceComplexity: O(V + E) for the adjacency list, the counts and the queue.

python3.referenceSolution:
from collections import deque


def finishableSteps(rules: list[int], steps: int) -> int:
    after = [[] for _ in range(steps)]
    waiting = [0] * steps
    for k in range(0, len(rules) - 1, 2):
        after[rules[k]].append(rules[k + 1])
        waiting[rules[k + 1]] += 1
    queue = deque(i for i in range(steps) if waiting[i] == 0)
    finished = 0
    while queue:
        step = queue.popleft()
        finished += 1
        for nxt in after[step]:
            waiting[nxt] -= 1
            if waiting[nxt] == 0:
                queue.append(nxt)
    return finished

problems.title: Beacon Code Contrast
problems.story: Rescue beacons along a coastline each broadcast a thirty-bit code. Two beacons are easiest to tell apart when their codes differ in as many high bits as possible, and the radio team wants the best pair before the next storm season.
problems.statement:
You are given the code broadcast by each beacon. Every code is a whole number from 0 to 1073741823, that is, at most thirty bits.

The contrast of two beacons is the bitwise exclusive or of their codes.

Return the largest contrast of any two different beacons. Two beacons can broadcast the same code; they are still different beacons, and their contrast is 0.
problems.inputFormat: Every number is the code of one beacon. There are at least two beacons.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the largest exclusive or of the codes of two different beacons.
constraints: Two beacons may broadcast the same code

examples.explanation: 19 is 10011 in binary and 12 is 01100, so they differ in all five bits and their exclusive or is 11111, which is 31. No pair can do better with five-bit codes.
There are only two beacons and they broadcast the same code, so their contrast is 0.
One code has every bit clear and the other has all thirty bits set, so every bit differs.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
The smallest and the largest code differ in every one of the thirty bits.
The fewest beacons, both broadcasting 0.
Two beacons whose codes share no set bit.
Five thousand codes near the top of the range: the top ten bits are set in every code, so the answer comes from the lower bits only.
Repeated codes: two beacons with the same code contrast by 0, so only a 9 against a 5 counts.
The largest code, 15, is not in the best pair: 8 against 7 gives 15, more than 15 against either.
Most codes share the 16 bit, so the best pair must include the one code without it.
Fifty-five hundred random thirty-bit codes; checking every pair is fifteen million comparisons.

hints: A higher bit is worth more than all the lower bits together. So decide the answer one bit at a time, from bit 29 down, always trying to set the current bit.
For a fixed code x, the best partner is found by walking down the bits of x and at each bit preferring a code that has the opposite bit, if one exists.

Store the codes in a binary trie keyed on their bits from the top. For each code, walk the trie choosing the opposite branch whenever it exists. Query each code before inserting it so a beacon is never paired with itself.

editorial.overview: The exclusive or is maximised greedily from the highest bit down, because winning a higher bit outweighs every lower bit. A binary trie over the codes answers, for each code, which partner wins the most high bits, in thirty steps.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Compute the exclusive or of every pair and keep the largest. That is n(n - 1) / 2 pairs, about five billion for the largest input.
editorial.optimalApproach: Keep a binary trie in which each code is a path of thirty bits, from bit 29 down to bit 0. Process the codes in order. For each code x after the first, walk the trie from the root: at each bit b of x, move to the child for 1 - b if it exists and add that bit to the running value; otherwise move to the child for b. Update the best value, then insert x. An equivalent approach without a trie builds the answer bit by bit: keep the set of every code's prefix on the bits decided so far, and keep the next bit only if some two prefixes exclusive-or to the candidate answer.
editorial.correctnessProof: For a fixed x, take any other inserted code y and let k be the highest bit where the walk's partner and y disagree. Above k they agree, so the walk had the same choice as y; at bit k the walk only avoids the opposite bit of x when no inserted code with the current prefix has it, so y cannot have it either, a contradiction unless the walk's partner is at least as good. So the walk finds x's best earlier partner. Every pair is seen when its later member is queried, and each code is queried before it is inserted, so it is only ever paired with a different beacon.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(30n): each code is queried and inserted along thirty levels.
editorial.spaceComplexity: O(30n) trie nodes in the worst case.

problems.title: Bead String Harvest
problems.story: At a craft fair game, a string of numbered beads hangs on a hook. Players pull beads off one at a time, and each pull scores more when the bead still has valuable neighbours. The stall owner wants to know the best score a perfect player could reach.
problems.statement:
You are given the value of each bead on a string, from left to right. Values can be 0.

Remove the beads one at a time, in any order, until none are left. Removing a bead scores its value multiplied by the value of the bead immediately to its left and the value of the bead immediately to its right at that moment. A neighbour that does not exist, because the bead is at an end of the string, counts as 1. After a removal, the two beads on either side become neighbours.

Return the largest total score you can reach.
problems.inputFormat: Every number is the value of one bead, in order along the string. There is at least one bead.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the largest total score.

parameters.name: beads
parameters.description: The value of each bead, left to right.

constraints: The answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer

examples.explanation: Remove the 4 first, scoring 2 x 4 x 3 = 24, which leaves 2 3. Remove the 2, scoring 1 x 2 x 3 = 6, then the 3, scoring 1 x 3 x 1 = 3. The total is 33, and no other order does better.
The only bead has no neighbours, so both count as 1 and the score is 1 x 5 x 1 = 5.
Remove the 0 first, scoring 0. Then remove the 2, scoring 6 x 2 x 1 = 12, and finally the 6, scoring 6. Removing the 6 while the 0 is still beside it would score nothing.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
A bead of value 0 earns nothing itself and wipes out any removal it borders.
One bead: both neighbours are missing and count as 1.
One bead of value 0 earns nothing.
The longest string, every bead at the largest value.
Equal beads: the order still matters, because the ends score less once their neighbours are gone.
Removing whichever bead scores the most right now gives only 26 here; the best order is worth far more.
Two natural greedy orders, smallest bead first and highest score now first, both fall far short of the best order.
A hundred and fifty random beads: trying removal orders is hopeless, and the cubic interval table is the intended cost.

hints: Deciding which bead to remove first is hard, because the neighbours of everything after it change. Instead, ask which bead in a stretch is removed last.

If bead k is the last one removed between two fixed beads l and r, then at that moment its neighbours are exactly l and r. The beads between l and k, and between k and r, are removed before it and never interact across k.

Pad the string with a 1 at each end. Let best(l, r) be the most you can score removing every bead strictly between l and r. Then best(l, r) is the maximum over k of best(l, k) + best(k, r) + value[l] x value[k] x value[r]. Fill the table by increasing gap.

editorial.overview: This is an interval dynamic program. The key move is to choose the last bead removed in a stretch, not the first: the last bead's neighbours are the fixed beads just outside the stretch, which splits the problem into two independent halves.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Try every removal order and score it. There are n! orders, which is hopeless beyond about ten beads.
editorial.optimalApproach: Build v with a 1 at each end: v = [1, beads..., 1]. Let dp[l][r] be the best score for removing every bead strictly between positions l and r, so dp[l][l + 1] = 0. For each gap from 2 up to n + 1, and each l, set r = l + gap and dp[l][r] = max over l < k < r of dp[l][k] + dp[k][r] + v[l] x v[k] x v[r]. The answer is dp[0][n + 1].
editorial.correctnessProof: Consider an optimal way to clear the beads strictly between l and r, and let k be the bead it removes last. Until then, k separates the beads on its left from those on its right, so their scores depend only on their own side, with l or k and k or r as the fixed outer neighbours; each side scores at most dp[l][k] and dp[k][r]. When k is finally removed its neighbours are l and r, scoring v[l] x v[k] x v[r]. So the optimum is at most the maximum in the recurrence, and every term of the recurrence is reached by clearing the left side optimally, then the right side, then k. Hence equality, and by induction on the gap every table entry is correct.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n^3): there are O(n^2) intervals and each tries O(n) last beads.
